# Amusement Park Profitability Case

[← Capital One](../README.md) · [Every Capital One question](../../capital-one.md) · [Read it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/study/amusement-park-profitability-case)

`critical-thinking` `open-ended` `verbal`

---

## Requirements

- Phase 1: conceptual opening — identify the drivers of an amusement park’s profitability: admission income, spending per guest inside the park, operating expenses, capacity limits, and seasonal demand.
- Phase 2: construct the P&L for an operating case provided by the interviewer, such as “a park with capacity for 5,000 people, open 200 days annually, and operating at 70% utilisation.” Cover revenue, variable expenses, fixed expenses, and net income. Some basic mental calculation is expected.
- Phase 3: run sensitivity or scenario checks — consider questions like “what if utilisation falls by 10%?” or “what ticket price produces break-even?” Determine which driver has the greatest effect.

## Notes

- The assessment focuses on organisation rather than exact arithmetic. Give the framework before calculating anything: `Profit = (Admissions Revenue + On-Site Revenue) - (Visitors × Variable Cost per Visitor + Fixed Costs)`. Many candidates begin multiplying without establishing this structure.
- Use approximate mental calculations because the interviewer wants sensible rounded reasoning, not precision. `5000 × 0.7 × 200 = 700,000 visitors/year` is sufficiently precise; working to four significant digits uses time without adding value.
- Candidate answers most often overlook the on-site spending driver, including food, merchandise, and photographs. Raising it without being prompted signals strong coverage of the business model.
- In sensitivity discussions, state the leading driver directly: for amusement parks, this is generally utilisation, because fixed costs create operating leverage, or spending per guest, because it carries a high margin. Express the elasticity in everyday language: “a 10% utilisation decline reduces margin more than proportionally because the fixed-cost base remains largely unchanged.”

## Preparation

- Rehearse the P&L breakdown until you can produce it automatically: start with revenue, move to costs, and divide both sides into two or three elements.
- Train with rounded-number mental maths: multiply two three-digit figures, divide a three-digit number by a two-digit number, and reach an answer within 10% of the exact result in 15 seconds.
- Practise a repeatable sensitivity format: identify the driver, indicate whether the effect is positive or negative, describe its approximate size as small, moderate, or large, and support that estimate with one sentence about operating leverage or unit economics.
